items.stem: In the chemical sense of the word, which of these samples is pure?

options.text: Distilled water, which contains only the compound H2O
Sea water, because it is clear and colourless
Spring water bottled with nothing added at all
Clean air, since each of the gases in it is pure

items.why: A pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance, and distilled water is only H2O.

items.stem: A student says carbon dioxide must be a mixture because it contains two different elements. Why is the student wrong?

options.text: It is a colourless gas, and colourless gases are pure
Carbon and oxygen are pure, so this gas is pure
Its atoms are chemically bonded in fixed proportions
Its elements are only mixed, not chemically bonded

items.why: A pure substance is a single element or compound, and in a compound the elements are chemically combined in fixed proportions.

items.stem: Which observation is the best evidence that a solid sample is pure?

options.text: It melts gradually over a range of several degrees
It melts sharply at one specific temperature
It is a fine white powder with no visible specks
It melts at a temperature well over 100 °C

items.why: Pure elements and compounds melt at specific temperatures, so a sharp melting point is the evidence wanted.

items.stem: A sample of sea water starts to boil at 102 °C and the temperature keeps rising while it boils. What does this show?

options.text: Salt gives the water a new fixed boiling point
The water in it is a different compound
It is pure, since nothing was added to it
It is a mixture, not a pure substance

items.why: Boiling over a range rather than at one specific temperature is how boiling point data reveal a mixture.

items.stem: A carton of milk is labelled pure milk. What does the word pure mean on that label?

options.text: It holds only one compound, so it is chemically pure
Nothing has been added to it, so it is in its natural state
It has been filtered until only water and fat are left
Every part of it looks the same, so it is one substance

items.why: In everyday language a pure substance is one that is unadulterated and in its natural state, eg pure milk.

items.stem: Pure aspirin melts at 135 °C. A student's prepared sample melts between 122 °C and 128 °C. What do the data show?

options.text: It is pure aspirin, since the average is close to the book value
It is pure, because pure solids melt over a range of degrees
It is impure, because an impurity raises the melting point
It is impure: the impurity lowered and spread the melting point

items.why: An impurity lowers a melting point and spreads it over a range, which is what these data show.

items.stem: Four liquids were heated to boiling. Which behaviour identifies a pure liquid?

options.text: It boils steadily at 78 °C until it has all gone
It boils at 100 °C and leaves a white solid behind
It boils away over a range from 78 °C to 91 °C
It starts to boil at 95 °C and the temperature rises

items.why: A pure compound boils at a specific temperature, which stays constant throughout boiling.

items.stem: Which of these is the definition of a formulation?

options.text: Any mixture containing two or more substances
A compound made by mixing elements together
A mixture designed as a useful product
A pure substance made to an exact recipe

items.why: This is the specification's definition: a formulation is a mixture that has been designed as a useful product.

items.stem: Why are the components of a formulation mixed in carefully measured quantities?

options.text: So the mixture becomes one pure compound as it is stirred
So the components all react and leave no waste behind
So the product has exactly the properties it was designed to have
They need not be measured; only the ingredients matter

items.why: The quantities are part of the design, and the proportions are what give the product its required properties.

items.stem: A student is given information about four substances. Which one is a formulation?

options.text: A paint with pigment, binder and solvent in fixed amounts
Sea water, a mixture of water and many different dissolved salts
Distilled water sold in bottles for topping up an iron
Nitrogen taken from air and used to fill food packets

items.why: Components with particular purposes, mixed in measured quantities to make a useful product, define a formulation.

items.stem: A jeweller melts 75% gold with measured amounts of copper and silver to make a harder gold alloy. Is the alloy a formulation?

options.text: No, because a formulation has to be a liquid such as a paint
No, because metals are elements, so alloys are pure
No, the metals join into a single pure metal
Yes: measured amounts are mixed to give a useful product

items.why: Components in carefully measured quantities give the required property, hardness, so this is a formulation.

items.stem: In paper chromatography, which phase is stationary and which is mobile?

options.text: Solvent stationary, the dyes are mobile
Paper stationary, solvent mobile
Paper stationary, the ink is mobile
Solvent stationary, the paper mobile

items.why: The paper never moves and the solvent rises through it, so the paper is stationary and the solvent mobile.

items.stem: Why do the substances in a mixture end up at different heights on a chromatogram?

options.text: Heavier substances are pulled back down the paper by gravity
The smallest particles fit through the gaps in the paper first
Each substance dissolves in a different part of the solvent
They are distributed differently between the paper and the solvent

items.why: Separation depends on the distribution of substances between the stationary and mobile phases.

items.stem: What does the Rf value of a compound compare?

options.text: The distance the spot moved up the paper, in centimetres
How far the compound moved against how far the solvent moved
How far the spot moved against the length of the paper
How far the solvent moved against how far the compound spot went

items.why: Rf is the ratio of the distance moved by the compound to the distance moved by the solvent.

items.stem: Which equation gives the Rf value of a substance?

options.text: Rf = distance moved by substance x distance moved up by solvent
Rf = distance moved by substance / total length of paper
Rf = distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent
Rf = distance moved by the solvent / distance moved by substance

items.why: This is the equation exactly as the specification gives it.

items.stem: A sample is run in three different solvents and gives one spot each time. What does this show?

options.text: The sample is a pure compound
The sample must be a single element
The spots have simply overlapped
Its Rf is the same in all three solvents

items.why: A pure compound produces a single spot in all solvents, which is what has been found here.

items.stem: Two dyes give the same Rf value in one solvent. What should the student do next?

options.text: Run them again in a different solvent and compare
Repeat the run in the same solvent for longer
Conclude that the dyes are the same compound
Decide that both of the dyes must be pure

items.why: Different compounds usually have different Rf values in a different solvent, so this tests the match.

items.stem: A dye is held strongly by the paper and dissolves only slightly in the solvent. On the chromatogram this dye will

options.text: travel with the solvent front, as dissolved dyes do
stay on the line, unable to enter the paper
move furthest of all, being the lightest one
move only a short way up, giving a low Rf value

items.why: Strong attraction to the stationary phase keeps the dye near the origin, so its Rf value is small.

items.stem: A chromatogram is run on a food colouring. Which result shows that the colouring is impure?

options.text: It gives a single spot, proving it is pure
The colouring separates into more than one spot
Its spot is bigger than the spot of the reference dye
Its Rf value differs from the reference dye's value

items.why: The compounds in a mixture separate into different spots, so several spots show the sample is impure.

items.stem: When finding an Rf value from a chromatogram, how is the distance moved by the substance measured?

options.text: From the bottom edge of the paper to the spot
From the pencil line to the top of the spot
From the pencil line to the spot's centre
From the pencil line to the very top of the paper

items.why: The specification defines the distance as the centre of the spot measured from the origin.

items.stem: On a chromatogram a spot has moved 3.6 cm from the pencil line and the solvent has moved 9.0 cm. What is the Rf value of the spot?

options.text: 5.4 cm, the difference of the two
2.5, worked out as 9.0 cm / 3.6 cm
0.40, worked out as 3.6 cm / 9.0 cm
0.40 cm, since Rf is a distance

items.why: R_f= (distance moved by substance) / (distance moved by solvent) = 3.6 / 9.0 = 0.40.

items.stem: A spot moved 2.7 cm and the solvent moved 5.9 cm. The calculator shows 0.457627 for the Rf value. How should the answer be given?

options.text: 0.46, matching the two significant figures measured
0.4576, since the extra digits make it more accurate
0.457627, exactly as the calculator displays it
0.5, rounded to just one significant figure

items.why: An answer is quoted to no more significant figures than the measurements it came from.

items.stem: In Required practical 6, why is the start line on the chromatography paper drawn in pencil?

options.text: Ink would react with the solvent to make a new dye
Pencil is easier to see against the coloured dyes
Pencil holds the spots in place on the line
Pencil does not dissolve and move up the paper

items.why: Pencil is insoluble in the solvent, so the line stays put instead of separating into spots of its own.

items.stem: Why must the solvent in the beaker start below the pencil line on the paper?

options.text: Otherwise the paper would sink to the beaker's base
Otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent
Otherwise the solvent front would end up uneven
Otherwise the solvent would rise too fast up the paper

items.why: Solvent above the line washes the samples off the paper instead of carrying them up it.

items.stem: A burning splint is held at the open end of a test tube of an unknown gas. Which observation shows that the gas is hydrogen?

options.text: The gas burns rapidly with a pop sound
The splint relights, burning brightly
The splint is put out straight away
The gas burns with a steady flame

items.why: This is the stated result of the hydrogen test: hydrogen burns rapidly with a pop sound.

items.stem: Which procedure and result together make up the test for hydrogen?

options.text: A glowing splint is inserted and then relights
Damp litmus paper is held in it and whitens
A burning splint at the open end gives a pop
A burning splint at the open end goes out

items.why: The test uses a burning splint held at the open end of the tube, and hydrogen burns rapidly with a pop sound.

items.stem: A glowing splint is inserted into a test tube of gas and the splint relights. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The gas is carbon dioxide, as it relights splints
The gas is oxygen, as it relights the splint
The relighting shows the gas is burning itself
The gas is hydrogen, as it relights splints

items.why: The splint relights in oxygen, so relighting identifies the gas as oxygen.

items.stem: Which splint and which result are used to identify oxygen?

options.text: A burning splint that then relights
A glowing splint that lights the gas
A burning splint that gives a pop
A glowing splint that relights

items.why: The oxygen test inserts a glowing splint into the tube and the splint relights.

items.stem: Limewater is used in the test for carbon dioxide. What is limewater?

options.text: An aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide
An aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide
An aqueous calcium carbonate solution
An aqueous calcium chloride solution

items.why: The specification defines limewater as an aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide.

items.stem: Carbon dioxide is bubbled through limewater. What is observed?

options.text: The limewater turns a bright yellow
The limewater is bleached white
The limewater stays unchanged
The limewater turns milky (cloudy)

items.why: The stated result is that the limewater turns milky (cloudy).

items.stem: Damp litmus paper is put into a test tube of chlorine gas. What happens to the paper?

options.text: It turns bright red and stays red
It turns green like the gas
It is bleached and turns white
It turns blue, showing an alkali

items.why: The stated result is that the damp litmus paper is bleached and turns white.

items.stem: Which observation identifies a gas as chlorine?

options.text: Damp litmus paper turns white
Dry litmus paper turns bright white
Damp litmus paper turns deep red
Limewater goes cloudy and milky

items.why: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper, so the paper turns white.

items.stem: A student holds a small sample of an unknown ionic compound on a clean wire in a hot Bunsen flame, and a strong colour appears. What does the flame colour identify?

options.text: the metal ion, the cation, present in that compound
the negative ion, the anion, in the compound
the compound as a whole and not one of its ions
the temperature reached by the Bunsen flame

items.why: Flame tests can be used to identify some metal ions (cations).

items.stem: Lithium chloride is held on a clean wire in a hot Bunsen flame. What is seen?

options.text: The flame turns a bright yellow colour.
The flame turns a deep crimson colour.
The flame turns an orange-red colour.
The flame turns a pale lilac colour.

items.why: Lithium compounds result in a crimson flame.

items.stem: Sodium chloride is used in a flame test. Which statement describes the result?

options.text: Sodium ions colour the flame bright orange.
Sodium ions colour the flame orange-red.
Sodium ions colour the flame yellow.
Sodium ions colour the flame lilac.

items.why: Sodium compounds result in a yellow flame.

items.stem: Potassium bromide is tested in a flame test. What is the result?

options.text: The flame colour produced is yellow.
The flame colour produced is crimson.
The flame colour produced is orange-red.
The flame colour produced is lilac.

items.why: Potassium compounds result in a lilac flame.

items.stem: Calcium nitrate gives a distinctive colour in a flame test. Which colour is it?

options.text: a pale green flame colour
an orange-red flame colour
a bright crimson colour
a bright yellow colour

items.why: Calcium compounds result in an orange-red flame.

items.stem: Copper(II) sulfate is held in a hot Bunsen flame during a flame test. What is seen?

options.text: The flame is coloured a crimson red.
The flame is coloured pale blue.
The flame is coloured a bright green.
The flame colour does not change at all.

items.why: Copper compounds result in a green flame.

items.stem: A solution contains both sodium ions and potassium ions. In a flame test only a yellow colour is seen. Why is the lilac colour of potassium not seen?

options.text: The potassium ions are destroyed in the flame.
The two colours mix to give a new colour.
Potassium needs a hotter flame than this one.
The intense sodium colour masks the lilac.

items.why: If a sample containing a mixture of ions is used some flame colours can be masked.

items.stem: An unknown compound gives a yellow flame test colour. Its solution gives a white precipitate when dilute hydrochloric acid and then barium chloride solution are added. What is the compound?

options.text: sodium sulfate
potassium sulfate
sodium carbonate
sodium chloride

items.why: The yellow flame shows sodium ions and the white precipitate with acidified barium chloride shows sulfate ions.

items.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of an unknown salt and a precipitate forms. Which ion in the salt does this test identify?

options.text: the negative ion in the salt, its anion
the hydroxide ion from the sodium hydroxide
the positive metal ion in the salt, its cation
both of the ions in the salt at one time

items.why: Sodium hydroxide solution can be used to identify some metal ions (cations).

items.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added, a few drops at a time, to separate solutions of aluminium ions, calcium ions and magnesium ions. What is seen in each tube?

options.text: A white precipitate forms in two of the tubes.
A coloured precipitate forms in each tube.
A white precipitate forms in one tube only.
A white precipitate forms in all three tubes.

items.why: Solutions of aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions form white precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added.

items.stem: Excess sodium hydroxide solution is now added to the three white precipitates formed from aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions. What happens?

options.text: Only the aluminium hydroxide dissolves.
Only the calcium hydroxide dissolves.
All three of the white hydroxides dissolve.
None of the three precipitates dissolves.

items.why: Only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution.

items.stem: Which set of metal ions all give coloured precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added to their solutions?

options.text: aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions
copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III)
copper(II), calcium and magnesium ions
aluminium, calcium and the iron(III) ion.

items.why: Solutions of copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) ions form coloured precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added.

items.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to iron(III) chloride solution. What is seen?

options.text: a green precipitate forms
a blue precipitate forms
a white precipitate is formed
a brown precipitate is seen

items.why: Iron(III) forms a brown precipitate.

items.stem: A solution gives a green precipitate when sodium hydroxide solution is added. Which ion does the solution contain?

options.text: The solution contains iron(II) ions.
The solution contains copper(II) ions.
It is a solution of iron(III) ions.
It is a magnesium salt in water.

items.why: Iron(II) forms a green precipitate.

items.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to copper(II) sulfate solution and a blue precipitate forms. Which equation for this reaction is correct and balanced?

options.text: CuSO4 + NaOH -> Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4
CuSO4 + 2NaOH -> Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4
2CuSO4 + 2NaOH -> 2Cu(OH)2 + 2Na2SO4
CuSO4 + 2NaOH -> CuOH + Na2SO4 + H2

items.why: Two hydroxide ions are needed for each Cu2+ ion, and every atom balances.

items.stem: Iron(II) sulfate solution reacts with sodium hydroxide solution to give a green precipitate. Which equation is correct and balanced?

options.text: Fe2SO4 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + Na2SO4
FeSO4 + NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4
FeSO4 + 2NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4
FeSO4 + 2NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4 + H2

items.why: Iron(II) is Fe2+, so the insoluble hydroxide is Fe(OH)2 and two NaOH are needed.

items.stem: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a white solid that is thought to be a carbonate. What is seen, and what gas is given off?

options.text: It fizzes, giving off carbon dioxide gas.
It fizzes, giving off hydrogen gas.
It fizzes, giving off oxygen gas.
It dissolves quietly, giving off no gas.

items.why: Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas.

items.stem: The gas given off when a carbonate reacts with a dilute acid is bubbled through limewater. What is the positive result?

options.text: The limewater relights a glowing splint.
The limewater turns cloudy, or milky.
The limewater turns a bright blue.
The limewater becomes colourless.

items.why: Carbon dioxide can be identified with limewater, which turns cloudy.

items.stem: Dilute nitric acid and then silver nitrate solution are added to a solution of an unknown halide. A cream precipitate forms. What does the solution contain?

options.text: The unknown solution contains chloride ions.
The unknown solution contains carbonate ions.
The unknown solution contains bromide ions.
The unknown solution contains iodide ions.

items.why: Silver bromide is cream.

items.stem: A solution is acidified with dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate solution is added. A yellow precipitate forms. Which ion is present?

options.text: the bromide ion, Br-
the chloride ion, Cl-
the sulfate ion, SO4 2-
the iodide ion, I-

items.why: Silver iodide is yellow.

items.stem: A student wants to show that a solution contains sulfate ions. What should be added, and what is a positive result?

options.text: dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution: a white precipitate
dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution: a white precipitate
dilute hydrochloric acid, then sodium hydroxide: a white precipitate
barium chloride solution alone: a cream coloured precipitate

items.why: Sulfate ions in solution produce a white precipitate with barium chloride solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid.

items.stem: Barium chloride solution is added to a solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid, and a white precipitate forms. What does this show?

options.text: Chloride ions are present in this solution.
Carbonate ions are present in solution.
Sulfate ions are present in the solution.
Barium ions are present in solution.

items.why: The white precipitate is barium sulfate, so sulfate ions are present.

items.stem: In Required practical 7 a student is given a solution of a single unknown ionic compound and must name it. Which plan will identify the compound?

options.text: adding sodium hydroxide, then more of it
adding barium chloride to test for chloride
just a flame test on its own is enough
a flame test, then a test for the anion

items.why: The compound is named only when both its metal ion and its negative ion have been identified.

items.stem: The specification describes instrumental methods of analysis. Which three words does it use?

options.text: accurate, sensitive and rapid
accurate and sensitive, but slow
cheap, simple and easy to carry
accurate, but far too slow to use.

items.why: Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.

items.stem: Give one advantage of using an instrumental method instead of the chemical tests in this specification.

options.text: It can be used without taking a sample at all.
It gives a result that never needs any checking.
It can detect a very small amount of a substance quickly.
It is always cheaper than a simple chemical test.

items.why: Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.

items.stem: Flame emission spectroscopy is an instrumental method. What is it used to analyse?

options.text: the non-metal ions present in solids
the non-metal ions dissolved in a solution
the mass of a solid sample taken
the metal ions present in solutions

items.why: Flame emission spectroscopy is used to analyse metal ions in solutions.

items.stem: In flame emission spectroscopy the sample is put into a flame. What happens to the light given out, and what is the output?

options.text: It passes into a spectroscope, giving a line spectrum.
It is split by a coloured filter into one colour.
It passes through a coloured filter, giving one colour.
It warms a sensor, giving a temperature reading.

items.why: The light given out is passed through a spectroscope and the output is a line spectrum.

items.stem: A student is given the line spectrum of a solution together with a reference set of line spectra for known metal ions. The sample spectrum contains every line of the lithium reference and every line of the calcium reference. What should the student conclude?

options.text: Only the ion with the brighter lines is present.
Lithium ions and calcium ions are both present.
Only the ion with the most intense lines is present.
Nothing can be concluded from a spectrum like this.

items.why: Each set of reference lines that appears in the sample spectrum shows that metal ion is present.

items.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to iron(III) chloride solution and a brown precipitate forms. Which equation is correct and balanced?

options.text: FeCl3 + 2NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + 2NaCl
FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + 3NaCl
FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + NaCl3
FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + 3NaCl

items.why: Fe3+ needs three hydroxide ions, and the three chloride ions give 3NaCl.

items.stem: A solution is analysed by flame emission spectroscopy. Sample lines (nm): 589, 671. Reference lines (nm): sodium 589; lithium 671; potassium 766; calcium 622. Which metal ions does the sample contain?

options.text: lithium and sodium ions
sodium ions on their own
sodium and potassium ions
potassium and calcium ions

items.why: Both reference lines, 589 nm and 671 nm, appear in the sample.
